prize_parts.citation: For establishing liquid-liquid phase separation as a physical-chemical principle that organizes the living cell into membraneless compartments

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensation is a new concept of molecular organisation: multivalent weak interactions drive thermodynamic demixing, giving compartments defined by phase behaviour, interfacial tension and material state rather than by membranes. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules are liquids (2009), and Rosen showed that multivalent signalling proteins undergo a sharp phase transition with a quantitative physical description (2012). Together they gave cell biology the vocabulary of phase diagrams, valency and viscoelasticity, and the idea has been tested in neurodegeneration, transcription, stress responses and protein aggregation. Fifteen years of independent work, including quantitative in vitro reconstitution, and a physical-chemical reading that chemists own, make this a chemistry prize in the same sense as earlier prizes for molecular organisation and self-assembly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field still argues about what counts as functional phase separation in vivo. Overexpression, in vitro crowding conditions and loose use of the word 'condensate' mean that some claims will not survive, and a prize can freeze a contested framing. Credit is also not clean: Pappu and Mittag supplied much of the sequence-grammar and thermodynamic framework, which a three-name slate cannot fully reflect, and part of the community would call the discovery cell biology rather than chemistry.

responses.point: Heiner ranks base editing first as a clean mechanistic principle with clinical benefit emerging, and puts phase separation third as somewhat premature because physiological relevance and quantitative criteria for condensates are still debated.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously and share part of it, but I would separate the discovery from its inflated applications. The liquid behaviour of P granules and the multivalent phase transition of signalling proteins are quantitatively reconstituted and have been reproduced many times; what is debated is how many cellular assemblies are truly equilibrium-like phase-separated. That is a normal maturation problem, not a doubt about the core claim. I also note that base editing arrives only six years after the 2020 genome-editing prize, which cuts against it as the recognition most urgently needed.

responses.point: Daniel ranks PROTACs and molecular glues first as a new pharmacological modality with clear design rules and a clinical pipeline, and stresses the test of whether chemists can now do something they could not before.
responses.response: I agree PROTACs pass that test conceptually, and it is a serious candidate. My hesitation is that no degrader is approved yet, and the credit is split between the PROTAC lineage and the thalidomide/cereblon molecular-glue lineage of Handa and Ito, which does not fit three names cleanly. Condensates instead change how we explain what happens inside cells, and I would argue that conceptual reach is the more durable test than a single modality. I would like to hear from Daniel how he would handle the Handa/Ito allocation.

responses.point: Johan puts machine-learned interatomic potentials first as a game-changer for atomistic simulation, and ranks energy-landscape folding theory third while noting its tie to the 2024 structure-prediction recognition.
responses.response: I share Johan's regard for the funnel picture, which I rank third, and I think it is overdue; the 2024 prize rewarded prediction and design, not the physical explanation of why proteins fold, so I do not see it as a duplication. On machine-learned potentials I am less convinced: the methods are impressive, but their consequences for chemical understanding are still mostly in production use rather than in resolved questions, and the attribution among Behler, Parrinello, Csanyi, Bartok and others is crowded. Computation has also been honoured in 2013 and 2024, so I would not make it the lead.

responses.point: Andrei ranks base editing first as a defined enzymatic chemistry turned into a programmable tool, and lists ionizable lipid nanoparticles third with a worry about overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize.
responses.response: We agree that base editing is mechanistically clean and that Liu is the decisive figure; my difference is mainly on whether a second editing prize so soon is the best use of the slot. On lipid nanoparticles I speak from my own field: the ionizable-lipid idea is real lipid physical chemistry, pKa-tuned charge, self-assembly and endosomal phase behaviour. I do not accept that the 2023 prize covers it, since that prize recognised RNA nucleoside modification, not delivery. My reservation is the same as his: attribution among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer is truly diffuse.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can word the prize so that it rewards the physical principle and the founding experiments without endorsing every claimed cellular condensate.
How to treat Pappu and Mittag relative to Rosen, since a three-name slate cannot cover the theory of sequence-encoded phase behaviour.
Whether colleagues from synthesis and analytical chemistry will accept a cell-biology-adjacent discovery as chemistry, and how that weighs against base editing or PROTACs.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I work in lipid and membrane physical chemistry and sit on the committee with Lund colleagues (Linke, Somfai), but no shortlisted candidate is a Lund colleague or collaborator that I know of. I note a field overlap with B058 (lipid nanoparticles) and B046 (phase behaviour of biomolecules), which I would disclose rather than treat as grounds for recusal.
